description: Test your knowledge of MI2.1-8 | Immunology: Basic, Applied & Immunological Disorders.

cards.text: What is the primary difference in timeline between innate and adaptive immunity?
cards.answer: Innate immunity acts within minutes to hours, while adaptive immunity develops over days to weeks. Innate is non-specific and has no memory; adaptive is antigen-specific with memory.

tip.tip: INNATE = FAST & FORGET; ADAPTIVE = SLOW & REMEMBER

cards.text: Define an epitope and explain its relationship to an antigen.
cards.answer: An epitope (antigenic determinant) is the specific region of an antigen recognized by an antibody or T-cell receptor. A single antigen molecule carries multiple epitopes.

tip.tip: Think of antigen as a building; epitope is the specific door antibodies recognize

cards.text: What is a hapten? Why is penicillin clinically important as a hapten?
cards.answer: A hapten is a small antigenic molecule that binds antibody but is not immunogenic alone; it requires coupling to a carrier protein. Penicillin acts as a hapten by binding to serum proteins, which is why it triggers allergic reactions.

tip.tip: Hapten = HALFgen; needs a PARTNER (carrier) to become immunogenic

cards.text: What is the major functional difference between thymus-dependent (TD) and thymus-independent (TI) antigens?
cards.answer: TD antigens require T-cell help to elicit antibody response and induce class switching and memory. TI antigens stimulate B cells directly without T-cell help, producing mainly IgM and no memory.

tip.tip: TD = needs THElper; TI = solo player. Polysaccharides are TI (poor vaccines in young children)

cards.text: What does the Fab region do, and what does the Fc region mediate?
cards.answer: Fab (Fragment antigen-binding) contains variable domains where antigen binds. Fc (Fragment crystallisable) mediates effector functions: complement activation, opsonization, ADCC, and placental transfer.

tip.tip: Fab = sticks to antigen (sticky); Fc = does the FunCtions

cards.text: How many heavy chains and light chains are in a single antibody molecule?
cards.answer: Two identical heavy (H) chains and two identical light (L) chains linked by disulfide bonds, forming a Y-shaped structure.

cards.text: Which antibody is the first to appear in a primary immune response, and why is it a poor indicator of acute infection in children?
cards.answer: IgM appears first in primary response and is the best complement activator. Polysaccharide vaccines are poorly immunogenic in children under 2 years because they trigger mainly IgM (TI antigen), which provides no memory.

tip.tip: IgM = Most (first); IgG = Good memory. Babies need protein antigens for lasting immunity

cards.text: Where is IgA most abundant, and what is its primary immune function?
cards.answer: IgA exists as a dimer in secretions (sIgA) and is most abundant in mucosal tissues (GI and respiratory tracts). Its primary function is mucosal defence at barriers.

tip.tip: IgA in secretions (milk, tears, saliva) = mucosAl immunity
